title: Boundaries
content_html:
Boundaries

Schemas and event segmentation

Schemas (representing prior knowledge) speed learning & consolidation by giving you a ready-made scaffold, so that new, congruent information slots in faster and consolidates sooner via mPFC-hippocampal interactions. In some cases this can compress systems consolidation to near one-shot learning. When new information fits what you already know, the brain needs less “binding” work; neocortical storage happens faster (often via mPFC guiding hippocampal encoding). This “rapid systems consolidation” has strong evidence in animal models and convergent support in humans.

Perception runs on prediction. Event segmentation relates to how the brain runs a “what’s happening now?” model to predict the next moments. Event segmentation carves experience into episodes - when prediction error or context change spikes (new goal/location/characters/tempo), you hit an event boundary. Boundaries act like chapter breaks: they reset/retune processing, boost within-event bindings, and weaken across-boundary links.

Schema ↔ boundary: strong schemas reduce prediction error (fewer boundaries; more gist-like encoding) until mismatch grows - then a boundary forces updating or new schema formation. This balances efficiency (schema-congruent compression) with sensitivity to change (novelty/distinctiveness). Schemas set expectations; mismatches or goal completions promote boundaries — so the two systems co-govern how episodes are carved and stored.

Temporal Context Models

As we experience things, the brain carries a slowly drifting temporal context - an internal representation of “now” that evolves continuously. Each new item (a word, image, event detail) gets bound to the current state of this context, and when one item is recalled, it reinstates its context, which cues recall of neighbors - explaining serial order and clustering in memory.

Event boundaries act like resets or sharp shifts in temporal context. Within an event, context drifts gradually (smooth linkage), whereas at a boundary, context jumps - so items before and after are less connected. This matches why people recall sequences within an event more tightly than across events.

Schemas act as context stabilizers by** reducing prediction error**, which stabilizes the temporal context and leads to fewer boundaries. A strong schema acts like a “gravitational pull” that keeps context steady until a violation forces a reset - this explains why well-structured narratives (with familiar schema) feel smoother and more coherent, while unfamiliar ones feel “choppier” with more boundaries.

Event segmentation explains discontinuity: boundaries punctuate experience into episodes. Schemas explain efficiency: when prior knowledge applies, encoding is compressed, boundaries reduced, and consolidation accelerated. Experience becomes structured memory through a dynamic balance of continuity (temporal context), discontinuity (boundaries), and efficiency (schemas).

Information flow

Are there any parallels between ‘event boundaries’ (memory) and ‘event horizon’ (black holes)?

Whilst there’s a useful metaphorical overlap, they’re not the same kind of thing. Both are boundaries that shape what information can carry forward - chapter breaks in memory vs. a causal “point of no return” in spacetime. However, memory boundaries are soft & probabilistic, triggered by prediction-error spikes and show hippocampal/arousal signatures; event horizons are hard & geometric, defined by spacetime curvature and no classical escape.

Conceptual Parallels

Information flow asymmetry. At a memory event boundary, associations and order memory drop across the break; the brain “resets” its event model. At a black hole’s event horizon, information can’t influence an outside observer-light itself can’t escape. In both, the boundary changes what information can carry forward.

Boundary-driven reorganization. Hippocampal activity peaks at cognitive boundaries and helps restructure episodes; in black holes, the horizon partitions spacetime into an inside/outside and sets what can, in principle, be learned from afar.

Observer’s effective model. Event segmentation depends on a person’s goals and knowledge; likewise, an external observer’s knowledge about a black hole is bounded by what reaches them from outside the horizon.

Information for Boundaries

Soft vs hard boundary. Memory boundaries are probabilistic-you can still link across them-whereas a classical event horizon is a one-way causal surface (escape velocity > c).

What causes them. Cognitive boundaries arise from prediction-error spikes during perception; horizons arise from spacetime geometry due to mass-energy, not prediction.

Dependence on the observer. Event boundaries vary with prior knowledge and goals; a black hole’s horizon is a geometric property of the spacetime (though identifying it locally is subtle).

Information for an observer is any physically realizable signal that changes the observer’s predictive distribution over a target variable. Quantify it with mutual information (MI) from Shannon. A memory event boundary involves** MI between pre- and post-boundary and features weakened but not forbidden links. A black-hole event horizon’s outside-accessible MI about inside states is ≈ 0 (classically) because no signals escape the horizon; entropy scales with area. Quantum accounts preserve unitarity but don’t give classical transmission across the horizon. This definition of information stays syntactic/physical (bits, prediction), avoiding semantic meaning debates while acknowledging Landauer’s “information is physical.” Philosophy of information reminds us that semantic/meaningful information is a different layer; we’re explicitly not relying on semantics for the cross-domain comparison.

Entropy

The brain doesn’t carry an inner “entropy gauge” or “mutual information meter” - those are formal constructs defined by scientists. But neural systems behave as if they track related quantities (surprise, prediction error, uncertainty), which can influence awareness (e.g., you feel surprised), even though the underlying information/entropy calculations are implicit and subpersonal. Shannon-style information is a tool we use to model those processes; it isn’t itself a conscious experience. The brain doesn’t explicitly “know” Shannon entropy or MI, but implements prediction-error, uncertainty, and efficient-coding computations that correlate with them. You consciously feel surprise or (un)certainty, not “entropy.”

Reflexive origins

Brains made these ideas, but reality constrains them. Abstract constructs (information, entropy, schemas, event boundaries) are invented formats for talking about regularities that brains discover. They stick around when they predict well, compress data, and respect physics (e.g., thermodynamic costs of information handling). Brains don’t do it alone; human cognition is extended through language, writing, diagrams, code, and instruments; culture tunes and transmits these “cognitive gadgets,” letting communities ratchet concepts over generations. We then use these made concepts to study the brain itself - e.g., event segmentation and schemas are scientist-built models validated by behavioral/neural signatures. So the notations are invented, the regularities (e.g., how uncertainty behaves in communication or memory) are discovered. That’s why these ideas travel across domains (information theory ↔ neuroscience) and survive new tests.
